voiceover.text: So, what happens when training stops? A rower breaks a wrist and can't row for six weeks. Their legs are fine, and there's a stationary bike. The coach says the six weeks are lost anyway, so rest completely and come back fresh. Do you agree? Write down why, in terms of what happens to the body in six weeks without training. Then say what you'd have the rower do instead.

scenes.title: reversibility: not everything is lost at once

voiceover.text: Reversibility is overload in reverse. Take away the stress, and the body sheds what it's no longer asked to keep, because keeping it costs energy. But things are lost at different rates. Fastest are blood plasma volume and stroke volume, measurably down within one to two weeks, so aerobic performance drops before the muscles have changed at all. Aerobic capacity falls more steadily, losing much of recent gains within four to eight weeks. Strength goes more slowly, and is often largely held for several weeks. Skill and technique are kept longest, for months or years. That last gap matters. A footballer coming back after a long break can still read the game and still do the skills, so they get into positions their fitness can't support. A returning athlete is unfit before they're unskilled, and that's where many comeback injuries start.

The other half of reversibility is maintenance. Holding an adaptation takes far less work than building it, often around a third of the usual training frequency, as long as intensity stays up. That's a maintenance load. So when volume has to fall, protect intensity. Now the rower. Their legs, heart and lungs can still be trained on the bike. That's cross-training, training a quality through a different activity. With a few hard bike sessions a week, most of their leg strength and aerobic fitness can be held. And since aerobic fitness is lost first, that's the priority to keep. So the six weeks aren't lost at all. The rower goes back fitter than if they'd rested, though they'll still ease back into rowing.

Variety is often written off as keeping training fun. Adherence does matter, because a program people quit produces nothing. But there are two physiological reasons too. An unchanging stress stops driving adaptation, which is the plateau from last time, from another angle. And repeating one movement loads the same tissues every session, which is how overuse injuries like shin pain and stress fractures develop. Here's the catch. Variety pulls against specificity. The answer is to vary the means, and hold the direction. A swimmer varies stroke, distance, equipment and intensity, but keeps training in the water. In aerobic training, variety often means changing surface or cross-training to spread impact. In strength training, it means changing exercises or tempo to keep a lift progressing.

A warm-up is a graded rise in temperature, circulation, range and readiness. Stage one is five to ten minutes of light, whole-body activity. It raises muscle temperature, heart rate and blood flow. Warmer muscle contracts and relaxes faster and is more pliable, and blood gives up oxygen to muscle more readily when it's warm. The heart also isn't asked for a sudden maximum from rest. Stage two is dynamic stretching through the ranges the session will use, as you saw earlier. Stage three is sport-specific skills at rising intensity, rehearsing movements and decisions. Stage four is mental preparation. For strength training, there's one more piece: warm-up sets of the actual lift with lighter loads, which rehearse the pattern as the weight climbs. A good warm-up reduces injury risk, especially for muscle strains, but it doesn't remove it.

scenes.title: the cool-down, and judging the three

voiceover.text: A cool-down runs the same sequence in reverse. Five to ten minutes of light activity keeps the muscle pump working, so blood doesn't pool in the legs and cause dizziness, and it helps clear by-products. Then static or PNF stretching while the tissue is warm, and fluid and food to start recovery. Now evaluate, because these three aren't equally supported. The warm-up has the strongest case, for both performance and injury. Variety is important, but only while specificity is kept. And the cool-down is the weakest. Its popular claim, that it stops next-day soreness, isn't well supported. Its value is the gradual return to rest and a chance to stretch. And all of them share one limit: the athlete's capacity to recover.
Two things to remember. When training must drop, reduce volume, protect intensity. And with variety, vary the means, hold the direction.

Two exam questions. First. A basketballer sprains an ankle and, for four weeks, does only upper-body weights. A lifter has done the same squat, with the same sets and tempo, every session for a year, and it has stopped improving. For each, name the principle, predict the consequence, and recommend a change. Pause here to answer.

The basketballer shows reversibility: aerobic fitness goes first, and weights don't train it. So add hard pool or arm-bike intervals. The lifter shows a lack of variety: the same stress no longer drives adaptation, so the plateau continues. Vary the exercise, tempo or sets, but keep the squat as the goal. The classic mistake is more of the same.
Second. A rugby team's pre-match routine is fifteen minutes of held static stretches, then kick-off. Evaluate this routine, and recommend a change. Pause here to answer.

It's a warm-up done in the wrong order and the wrong place. Muscle temperature and heart rate barely rise, nothing rehearses the game, and long static holds right before explosive play may cut power. So start with light running, then dynamic stretching, then rugby skills at rising intensity, and move the static work to the cool-down. The classic mistake is saying they had no warm-up.

So when training stops, hold intensity and keep what's lost first. Vary the means, not the direction. And warm up and cool down for their mechanisms, not habit. Watch the heart rate settle back to rest. In a trained athlete it settles at forty-eight. In an untrained person, seventy-two. That gap is a training adaptation.
